name: Zapoteco de San Juan Coatecas Altas
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 5 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: [p.53] El acento recae en la última sílaba en casi todas las raíces acentuadas de esta variante del zapoteco. Como los pronombres dependientes no tienen acento, en general se escriben separados de la raíz para mantener el patrón del acento de las raíces, aunque estos pronombres actúan como sufijos. Solamente se escriben como parte de la raíz si empiezan con una vocal. Los pronombres que empiezan con vocales son los de la primera y segunda persona del singular, y los de la tercera persona del singular inanimada. ... Los siguientes ejemplos tienen lizh hogar (casa): lizha mi casa / lizhal tu casa / lizh xaꞌ su casa (respeto) ... lizhe su casa (objeto). [p.43] 3. Notas acerca de las sílabas acentuadas. En las palabras compuestas, la sílaba acentuada que está más a la derecha es la que recibe el acento principal. Ejemplos: ntsiki echar lumbre / niliwen sanar. [p.41] La vocal o del zapoteco de Coatecas Altas tiene varias pronunciaciones. En sílabas acentuadas y abiertas, se pronuncia como el desliz [ʊo]. En otras sílabas acentuadas, su pronunciación varía entre [u], [ʊ] y [o]. En sílabas no acentuadas, se pronuncia [u] y se escribe u. new_statements.quote: [p.43] 3. Notas acerca de las sílabas acentuadas. En las palabras compuestas, la sílaba acentuada que está más a la derecha es la que recibe el acento principal. Ejemplos: ntsiki 'echar lumbre', niliwen 'sanar'. [p.41] La vocal o del zapoteco de Coatecas Altas tiene varias pronunciaciones. En sílabas acentuadas y abiertas, se pronuncia como el desliz [ʊo]. En otras sílabas acentuadas, su pronunciación varía entre [u], [ʊ] y [o]. En sílabas no acentuadas, se pronuncia [u] y se escribe u. Ejemplos: yo 'tierra' (se pronuncia [yʊo]) ... ngot 'muerto' (se pronuncia [ngʊot] o [ngut]), ngubizh 'sol' (se pronuncia [ngubizh]).
new_statements.translation: [p.43] 3. Notes on stressed syllables. In compound words, the stressed syllable that is furthest to the right is the one that receives the primary stress. Examples: ntsiki 'to make a fire', niliwen 'to heal'. [p.41] The vowel o of Coatecas Altas Zapotec has several pronunciations. In stressed open syllables it is pronounced as the glide [ʊo]. In other stressed syllables its pronunciation varies between [u], [ʊ] and [o]. In unstressed syllables it is pronounced [u] and written u. Examples: yo 'earth' [yʊo] ... ngot 'dead' [ngʊot]~[ngut], ngubizh 'sun' [ngubizh].

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only explicit placement rule is for compounds: primary stress goes to the rightmost member's stressed syllable, i.e. toward the end of the word. For non-compound words the source gives no rule in words, but its example ngubizh 'sun' (prefix ngu- written with unstressed u, root bizh stressed) shows prefix syllables unstressed and the root — the final syllable in native vocabulary, since post-tonic vowels have been lost (Beam de Azcona 2023) — stressed. Loanword adaptation (Valenzuela Romo 2013: post-tonic syllables deleted, oxytone loans kept) and Juárez Santiago 2018 (compound prominence on the last member) point the same way: word-final (= root) stress. Reading 'fixed: final syllable' is an inference from these converging partial statements, not a sentence any source states for simplex words; 'morphologically determined' would be an equally defensible label.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Implied only: non-final members of compounds retain their own 'sílaba acentuada' while the rightmost one gets the 'acento principal'; nothing further said.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Unadapted Spanish loans keep Spanish stress (Valenzuela Romo 2013 pp.43-44, e.g. [ti.bu.'ron], [ka.'fe]). The independent 'sílaba fuerte / sílaba normal' contrast (Benton pp.43-44: shorter vowel, higher pitch, sometimes rapid intensity drop) is a lexical syllable-type contrast on the stressed syllable, not a stress-placement matter; five lexical tones are independent of stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (orthographic/citation forms in a vocabulary); explicit statement restricted to compound words; the language is tonal (5 tones per Benton, 4 per Juárez Santiago) with stress mentioned separately from tone; native roots are overwhelmingly monosyllabic with unstressed (often toneless) prefixal/pre-tonic syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: All three primary sources describe the speech of the town of San Juan Coatecas Altas (Ejutla district, Oaxaca) = Glottolog coat1244 / ISO zca exactly (Valenzuela also mentions the migrant colony San Bernardino on the coast). Beam de Azcona (2018 INALI talk; 2023) treats Coatecas Altas as a variety of Amatec / Dí'zhzêh together with San Cristóbal Amatlán (Glottolog amat1238, ISO zpo), reported mutually intelligible; Glottolog keeps them as separate languages under Macrocoatecano. Autonym dix̲zë̂ (Juárez Santiago) / di'zhzë (Benton).

tone_statements.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2023 [issue dated 2024]. The tonal morphology of the potential in Coatec Zapotec (Di′zhke′): implications for early Zapotecan tone, *ʔ, and verb classes through internal and comparative reconstruction. Journal of Historical Linguistics 14(2): 179-241. Amsterdam: John Benjamins. (Author's preprint: rosemarybeamdeazcona.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/)
tone_statements.quote: San Agustín Mixtepec lacks a falling tone in general, but Coatecas Altas has the same tonal inventory as Coatec when it comes to modal vowels. This is to say that Coatecas Altas has a falling tone on many or most of the same words that have a falling tone in Coatec, presumably from an HL melody on an earlier disyllable. ... Amatec and Miahuatec both have a rising tone that occurs on modal syllables ... Coatecas Altas, and at least the San Bartolomé Loxicha variety of Miahuatec, only have low and high tone on glottalized syllables, even though they have a larger inventory on modal vowels.
tone_statements.locator: preprint p. 26, §4.4.1 'Synchronically glottalized verbs'; Coatec reference inventory ex.(8) 'High (H), Low (L), Falling (HL), Rising (LH), Glottal' on p. 9, §3
tone_statements.summary: Inventory stated as identical to Coatec's listed modal-vowel tones (H, L, falling, rising); only H vs L on glottalized syllables; pre-tonic syllables toneless. Count 4 rests on that equation.

tone_statements.quote: To date, I have found five contrastive tones in CAZ: Low, Mid, High, Rising and Falling. Though I have the fewest examples for Mid tone, all five tones are in contrast on unlaryngealized and laryngealized roots: ... One other phonemically contrastive feature closely associated with tone is what I choose to call syllable intensity. High-intensity syllables tend to phonetically raise tones, shorten vowels, and harden laryngealization into a phoneticaly strong glottal stop.
tone_statements.locator: §4.2 Tone & syllable intensity, sketch p.7; inventory restated §5 p.11: 'Tones: Low (4), Mid (3), High (1), Rising (41) and Falling (14)'
tone_statements.summary: Five root tones (L, M, H, rising, falling) plus a high/low 'syllable intensity' (2004 paper: tone register) contrast, with F0/duration measurements; stress non-contrastive, root-final.

tone_statements.quote: Laryngealization, tone, syllable intensity and nasalization are the four types of contrastive suprasegmental features I have currently found in CAZ. Though stress is not contrastive, I discuss it first, since I had originally thought it was. [...] 4.1 Stress. On polysyllabic roots in CAZ, stress always falls on the ultimate syllable.8 Apparent exceptions involve roots with a final first person singular (1sg.) clitic pronoun. [fn. 8: Clitic suffixes are usually not stressed.] [...] 4.2 Tone & syllable intensity. To date, I have found five contrastive tones in CAZ: Low, Mid, High, Rising and Falling.

tone.quote: En el zapoteco sureño las vocales átonas se han perdido en la historia, aunque nuevas vocales átonas surgen en préstamos del español, y en palabras compuestas. Las nuevas sílabas átonas difieren de las sílabas tónicas por su falta de contrastes tonales. La monosilabicidad es fuerte en lenguas macrocoatecanas, miahuatecanas y cisyautepequeñas.
tone.translation: In Southern Zapotec the unstressed vowels have been lost historically, although new unstressed vowels arise in loans from Spanish and in compound words. The new unstressed syllables differ from the stressed syllables in their lack of tonal contrasts. Monosyllabicity is strong in Macro-Coatecan, Miahuatecan and Cis-Yautepecan languages.
